Abstract: The exchange of biological matter between bacterial cells drives adaptation and evolution. However, whether bacteria can exchange functional proteins remains unclear. Here, we show that antibiotic treatment induces vesicle-mediated horizontal protein transfer within and between bacterial species. By combining a genetic system in Escherichia coli to track transfer events with single-cell transcriptomic profiling, we found that antibiotics stimulate the differentiation of an isogenic bacterial population into distinct transient cell states: donor cells that activate a membrane stress response to release protein-containing vesicles, and recipient cells that suppress this response to take up vesicle contents. This antibiotic-induced protein exchange enables dormant persister cells to acquire proteins from active neighbors, enhancing survival and revealing a previously unrecognized mechanism by which bacteria withstand antibiotic treatment.

Main Text:

The horizontal exchange of biological material drives prokaryotic evolution and the spread of

antibiotic resistance (1). It also enables interspecies competition and commensalism in nutrient-

limited environments (2, 3). However, beyond proteins delivered by specialized secretion

systems (4-6), it remains unclear whether functional proteins can translocate from one bacterium

to another.

Bacterial membrane vesicles, which are lipid nanoparticles that can be derived from outer and

inner membranes, and which can contain membranous, periplasmic, and cytosolic contents (7,

8), have been proposed to mediate the exchange of biological material, including protein,

between bacteria (9, 10). The incubation of bacteria with vesicle-enriched samples, derived from

concentrated culture supernatant, has been associated with adaptive behaviors such as nutrient

uptake and horizontal gene transfer (HGT) (9, 11, 12). Furthermore, the velocity and diffusivity

of vesicles increase during antibiotic treatment (13), suggesting that certain stresses might

promote vesicle-mediated material exchange (9, 13). However, prior readouts of vesicle-

mediated exchange, such as changes in recipient viability or acquisition of donor resistance

genes, are indirect and nonspecific (9, 12, 14-18). These readouts can be influenced by other

particles, including bacteriophages, that can co-purify with pelleted vesicles (9, 19).

Additionally, no genetic regulators of vesicle-mediated exchange have been identified, casting

further doubt on whether the phenotypes observed in these studies are truly vesicle-mediated (9,

20). Therefore, a sensitive and trackable method is needed to study material exchange by

membrane vesicles.

To label transfer events, we constructed a Cre-loxP genetic system in Escherichia coli consisting

of a donor and a recipient strain (21). The donor strain cannot ferment galactose (Gal-) due to a

deletion of the galK gene and carries a chromosomal arabinose-inducible cre gene encoding the

site-specific Cre recombinase, which selectively recombines loxP DNA sequences. The recipient

strain carries a galK gene with a portion that is inverted (21), abolishing galactokinase activity

regardless of the direction of transcription, and this inversion is flanked by opposing loxP sites.

If Cre recombinase activity is transferred from donors to recipients, the loxP sites will

recombine, and the resulting reversion of the galK gene will restore galactokinase activity and

allow recipient cells to grow on galactose (Gal+) (Fig. 1A).

When we co-incubated donors and recipients, we found that Gal+ colonies emerged at a

frequency of 3.4 x 10-7 recipients. Furthermore, transfer was dependent on donor Cre expression,

and colony PCR confirmed the Gal+ colonies’ identities as loxP-reverted recipients (Fig. 1B-C,

fig. S1A-B). To test whether Gal+ recipients can arise from DNA transfer, recipients were

incubated with purified cre DNA. No transfer events were detected except in the case of forced

DNA uptake by electroporation (fig. S1C), excluding DNA as a source of Cre transfer.

As vesicle production can be stimulated by fluoroquinolones (13, 22), we tested the effect of

ciprofloxacin treatment on Cre transfer. Treating donors and recipients with the minimum

antibiotic concentration (MAC) of ciprofloxacin (8.5 ng/mL for wild-type E. coli; MAC of

ciprofloxacin abbreviated as cip hereon), a sub-inhibitory concentration that reduces the 16 hour

culture titer by 90% (23) (Table S4), enhanced the frequency of Cre transfer > 4000-fold (Fig.

1C). Ciprofloxacin induction was synergistic, as treating either donors or recipients alone

produced only modest increases in transfer (fig. S2A). The effect of ciprofloxacin induction

plateaued at the MAC, resulting in a transfer frequency of ~1.4 x 10-3 recipients, and additional

The induction of horizontal transfer was not exclusive to fluoroquinolones, and intercellular

transfer extended beyond E. coli MG1655. When donors and recipients were induced with the

Cre to E. coli (Fig. 1D). High frequency transfer by P. putida donors depended on donor Cre

expression and recipient cip induction, and P. putida transfer frequencies were comparable to E.

coli donors. Interestingly, P. putida possessed high Cre transfer activity even without antibiotic

induction. These data suggest that the horizontal Cre transfer is a generalized phenomenon that

can occur across different classes of antibiotics as well as bacterial strains lacking cryptic

prophages and other bacterial species.

Recipients express markers of cell dormancy

Because the Psp regulon is required for efficient vesicle-mediated HPT in donors, we tested its

role in recipients. Deleting pspA in recipients reduced Cre uptake by >5,000-fold during cip

treatment (Fig. 4B). Unexpectedly, this defect was fully rescued by deleting the entire regulon

(Δpsp) (Fig. 4B). As PspA suppresses Psp expression by inhibiting the transcription factor PspF,

these results suggested that suppression of Psp activity promotes protein uptake. Moreover, a

PspF G94E mutant defective in transcription factor function (fig. S9A) (47) rescued the loss of

protein uptake observed in ∆pspA recipients, and protein uptake was reduced in recipients

overexpressing PspC (Fig. 4B). Therefore, whereas donors require Psp activation for transfer,

recipients require Psp suppression to become protein-competent.

## Discussion

Here, we identified vesicle-mediated horizontal protein transfer (HPT) as form of bacterial

material exchange that occurs within and between gram-negative species. Using Escherichia

coli, we showed that antibiotic stress activates this exchange by inducing two opposing cell

states within an isogenic population: donors that release protein-filled vesicles and recipients that

take up vesicle contents. These unidirectional transfer events arise from antibiotic-driven

regulatory program divergence. The Cre–loxP reporter system allowed us to visualize this

process and reveal how antibiotics orchestrate vesicle production, uptake, and intercellular

protein trafficking (Fig. 5J).

In donors, the activation of the Psp response promotes the production of HPT vesicles (Fig. 5J).

The Psp response was discovered during phage infection, but it has since been associated with

protection from a wide variety of perturbations that disrupt inner membrane integrity and proton

motive force (41, 60, 61). We show that in addition to Psp’s protective properties at the

intracellular level, it confers benefits at the intercellular level by enabling the sharing of vesicle

contents among a population. PspA, a member of the conserved ESCRT-III–like membrane

remodeling protein, relocates from the cytoplasm to the inner membrane upon Psp activation and

is detectable in transfer vesicles (39, 62). ESCRT-III proteins are known to promote vesicle

budding in eukaryotes (63). As pspA deletion alone does not significantly reduce HPT vesicle

production, while the deletion of all Psp genes does, other Psp proteins may be functionally

redundant to PspA during HPT vesicle production in E. coli (Fig. 3H). The enrichment in HPT

vesicles of Cre, PspA, and phosphatidylglycerol, which PspA is known to preferentially bind to

(45), suggests that vesicle contents are selectively packaged and released. Prior studies have

demonstrated that Gram-negative bacteria produce vesicles containing inner membrane and

cytoplasmic material, likely through membrane fragmentation and recircularization or

coordinated budding of both outer and inner membranes (64, 65). Local increases in

phosphatidylglycerol content along portions of donor cell membrane could act as binding sites

for PspA, and these sites eventually form transfer vesicles either through membrane budding or

fragmentation.

In recipients, suppression of the Psp response promotes vesicle uptake. This trade-off in

reduction of membrane stress protection in exchange for uptake suggests that vesicle acquisition

provides a survival benefit. Consistently, we found that Psp suppression and vesicle uptake are

linked to enhanced antibiotic persistence through increased HipA expression. Single-cell RNA-

seq revealed opposing hipA and ribosomal gene expression signatures in donors and recipients.

Together with the finding that elevated HipA suppresses donor transfer while promoting

recipient uptake, this indicates that HipA activity helps determine whether cells within an

isogenic population adopt donor or recipient states. As HipA is suppressed by physical

association with the HipB repressor (66), it is possible that spontaneous changes in intracellular

HipB levels can lead to bistable switching between the donor and recipient cell states.

Increased vesicle exposure prior to lethal antibiotic treatment enhances antibiotic persistence.

Uptake of key proteins, such as ribosomal components, metabolic enzymes, or DNA repair

factors, from active neighbors may help persisters endure proteome-damaging stress despite

reduced protein synthesis. Alternatively, vesicle-derived proteins or signaling molecules may

further reinforce dormancy in competent cells. Indeed, prior studies have found that quorum

sensing molecules can be packaged into vesicles in Pseudomonas aeruginosa (67). Strategies to

reduce antibiotic persistence may involve disrupting horizontal protein transfer or redirecting this

pathway to deliver toxic cargo to persister cells.

Although our study focuses on E. coli, the observation of cross-species transfer suggests that

protein exchange may be widespread in microbial communities. HPT could create protein-

sharing networks that enhance collective adaptability under stress or, alternatively, promote

interbacterial competition. Understanding the ecological and evolutionary roles of intra- and

interspecies protein transfer will provide new insight into how bacterial communities persist in

hostile environments.

## Materials and Methods

Bacterial strains and growth conditions

Escherichia coli MG1655 and Pseudomonas putida KT2440 were used for all experiments. Cultures were streaked onto LB plates supplemented with antibiotics when necessary for plasmid maintenance. Single colonies were picked and inoculated into 3 mL of LB-Lennox media. For E. coli donors, liquid culture was supplemented +/-0.2% arabinose for Cre induction and +/- ciprofloxacin to induce transfer. For P. putida donors, liquid culture was supplemented 40 µg/mL kanamycin for plasmid maintenance, 1000 ng/mL ATc for Cre induction, and +/- ciprofloxacin to induce transfer. For E. coli recipients, liquid culture was supplemented +/- ciprofloxacin to induce transfer. Cultures were grown at 37°C. The minimum antibiotic concentration (MAC) was identified separately for each strain (Supplementary Table 1).

Colony PCR

Individual colonies were picked off the plate and directly added to GoTaq® Hot Start Green Master Mix (Promega M512C) with the appropriate primers. Amplification was performed per manufacturer instructions and bands were analyzed using the Azure C200 Gel Imaging Workstation where appropriate.

Supernatant isolation

Donor culture was harvested at exactly 16 hrs post-inoculation. Cells were pelleted in 1.5 mL Eppendorf tubes, and 3 mL of supernatant was extracted and filtered by a 0.2 µm surfactant-free cellulose acetate filter (Corning 431219).

Donor-recipient cell and supernatant co-incubations

Cultures were grown as previously described and harvested at exactly 16 hours post-inoculation. To determine the frequency of cell-cell transfer, 500 uL of donor culture was combined with 500 uL of recipient culture, resuspended in 100 uL of LB + 0.2% arabinose, and incubated for 1 hr at 37°C. For multi-hour cell-cell co-incubations in sublethal or lethal antibiotics, 250 uL of donor culture was combined with 250 uL of recipient culture and resuspended in 500 uL of LB + 0.2% arabinose with the appropriate concentration of antibiotics. For cell-protein co-incubations, 500 uL of recipient culture was resuspended in 100 uL of LB + 0.2% arabinose and purified Cre recombinase (NEB M0298L) was added. Samples were then incubated for up to 24 hours at 37°C. To determine the frequency of supernatant-cell transfer, 500 uL of recipient culture was resuspended in 100 uL of donor supernatant and incubated for 1 hr at 37°C. After co-incubations, mixtures were washed and resuspended in 500 uL of 1x MinA media + 1 mM MgSO4. Gal+ quantification was assessed by plating co-incubation mixtures onto 1x MinA plates supplemented with + 1 mM MgSO4 and 0.2% galactose at 37°C. Sodium dodecyl sulfate, nonylphenyl etheoxylate, loxP plasmid DNA, or Pronase was spiked into cell-cell or cellsupernatant co-incubation mixtures where applicable. Donor supernatant was pre-treated at 37°C for an hour with Pronase prior to co-incubation with recipients where applicable. All experiments were replicated a minimum of three times in the laboratory.

DNA co-incubation and electroporation

Donor genomic DNA was isolated from donor cultures with the Wizard® Genomic DNA Purification Kit (Promega A1120). 125 ng/uL of genomic DNA was fragmented for 3 hrs at 37°C with Fastdigest EcoRI (Thermo Scientific™ FD0274), then heat-inactivated at 80°C. Amplicons of the cre locus were prepared by performing colony PCR with Phusion Hot Start II DNA Polymerase (Thermo Scientific™ F549L) using primers located upstream and downstream of the cre gene as recorded in Supplementary Table 2. Genomic and amplicon samples were purified with the QIAquick PCR Purification Kit (Qiagen 28104). AraC+ recipient culture was grown as previously described and harvested at 16 hrs post-inoculation. 10 uL of fragmented DNA or 100 ng of cre locus amplicon was co-incubated with 500 uL of recipient culture resuspended in 100 uL of LB + 0.2% arabinose for 1 hr at 37°C. The mixture was then resuspended and plated as described before for other co-incubations. For electroporation, AraC+ recipient culture was grown as previously described and harvested at 16 hrs post-inoculation, then diluted 1:100 in 100 mL of LB + 0.2% arabinose. Cultures were grown at 37°C until OD600 reached 0.4, then washed 3x with ice-chilled water before being resuspended in 1 mL of water. 50 uL of electrocompetent cells were electroporated with 2 uL of fragmented genomic DNA or 50 ng of cre locus amplicon using the BioRad Gene Pulser® II set to 1.4 kV. Cells were recovered in 1 mL LB-Lennox media for 1 hr at 37°C, diluted as necessary, and plated onto LB media for titers and 1.5% agar 1x MinA plates supplemented with 0.2% galactose + 1 mM MgSO4 for quantification of Gal+ frequency. All experiments were replicated a minimum of three times in the laboratory.

Western blotting and mass spectrometry

Cultures were grown as previously described. Protein was precipitated with 10% trichloroacetic acid and 0.015% sodium deoxycholate where necessary for samples with low protein concentrations. Protein pellets were resuspended in 100 uL of 2x Laemmli buffer with 1% betamercaptoethanol and neutralized with Tris-HCl. 10 uL of each sample were loaded into 10% Mini-PROTEAN® TGX™ Precast Protein Gels (BioRad 4561035) and run at 200V for 40 min. Lanes were transferred onto PVDF membranes using the Trans-Blot Turbo Mini 0.2 µm PVDF Transfer Packs (BioRad 1704156) and Trans-Blot Turbo Transfer System following the mixed molecular weight protocol. Membranes were blocked in 2% milk TBS-Tween 0.2% overnight at 4°C. Primary antibody was added to the blocking buffer (1:5,000 dilution for Cre recombinase Polyclonal Antibody, Invitrogen PA5-32244; 1:10,000 dilution for in-house rabbit polyclonal GroEL antibody) and incubated overnight at 4°C. Blots were washed 3x 5 min with TBS-Tween 0.2% at room temperature, then the secondary antibody was added (1:10,000 dilution, Goat antirabbit polyclonal Cy5, Invitrogen A10523) and incubated at room temperature for 1 hr, then washed 3x 5 min with TBS-Tween 0.2% and resuspended in TBS. Fluorescence signal was detected using the Azure C400 Gel Imaging system. Quantification of western blots was performed using FIJI (68) image processing package. For mass spectrometry, protein pellets were washed twice with 200 uL ice-cold acetone and air-dried for 10 min. Samples were submitted to the Baylor College of Medicine mass spectrometry core (RRID:SCR_027015) for analysis. Intensity based absolute quantification (iBAQ) was used to quantify protein abundance. Hierarchical protein clustering based on fraction of total protein abundance normalized separately across F2-F6 and across Cells and Sup was performed using the default settings of ComplexHeatmap v2.16.0 in R. Proteins absent from >1 replicate in each fraction or from >2 fractions were excluded from clustering.

Lipid extraction and analysis

Vesicle fractions (~1 mL) were mixed with 1 mL methanol and 2 mL chloroform, vortexed and incubated on nutating shaker for 15 mins. Extraction mixture was centrifuged at 1000 g for 10 mins. Bottom organic layer was collected. Top aqueous layer was acidified with 20 mL formic acid and re-extracted with 2 mL chloroform. Bottom organic layer from both steps were pooled and dried under N2 stream. Dried lipids were re-suspended in 50 mL 2:1 chloroform: methanol, 10 mL was injected on SHIMADZU Nexera UHPLC coupled with SCIEX ZenoTOF 7600 mass spectrometer. Chromatographic separation was achieved on C18 reverse phase column (Pheneomenex, 5 μm, 50 x 4.6 mm #00B-4435-E0). Solvent = 60:40 (v/v) ACN/water + 0.1% (v/v) formic acid + 10 mM ammonium formate, Solvent B = 90:10 (v/v) IPA: ACN + 0.1% (v/v) formic acid + 10 mM ammonium formate. Separation gradient started with 10% B for 0.5 mins, followed by a linear increase to 100% B from 0.5 to 25 mins, 100% B maintained at 28 mins, 10% B at 28.01 mins, 10% B maintained till 30 mins. Column temperature was maintained at 600C, and flow rate was maintained at 0.5 mL/min throughout the separation. ZenoTOF parameters were as follows: curtain gas = 45, CAD gas = 9, ion Source gas 1 = 40 psi, ion source gas 2 = 70 psi, temperature = 450 0C, spray voltage = -4500 V for negative mode and 5500 V for positive mode. TOF start mass = 200 Da, TOF stop mass = 2000 Da, accumulation time = 0.1 s, delustering potential = -40 V for negative mode and 40 V for positive mode, collision energy = - 12 V for negative mode and 12 V for positive mode, QJect RF amplitude = 193.78 V. MS/MS was acquired with CID fragmentation, TOF start mass = 100 Da, TOF stop mass = 2000 Da, accumulation time = 0.005 seconds, collision energy = -60V for negative mode and 60 V for positive mode with collision energy spread of 20 V, QJect RF amplitude = 202.72 V. Raw files were analyzed with MS-DIAL4.90, with  following parameters: MS1 tolerance = 0.01 Da, MS2 tolerance = 0.025 Da, peak detection = 1000 amplitude, mass slice width = 0.1 Da, MS2 deconvolution: sigma window value = 0.5, ms/ms abundance cutoff=0, ms/ms identification score cutoff = 80%. For alignment, retention time tolerance = 0.05 mins and MS1 tolerance = 0.015 Da. Lipids with no tandem mass fragment were removed. Area under the curve was used for quantitation. PG and Cardiolipin were analyzed in negative mode and PE were analyzed in positive mode. Lipid extraction and analysis were performed once with three independent biological replicates. Hierarchical clustering of lipid species by the relative abundance of each species normalized to total lipid in each fraction was performed using the default settings of ComplexHeatmap v2.16.0 in R.

RT-qPCR and bulk RNA sequencing Cultures were grown as previously described. Total RNA was harvested using the RNASnapTM protocol (69). RNA Clean & Concentrator Kit (Zymo Research) with on-column DNAse I digestion was performed and samples were resuspended in nuclease-free water. For RT-qPCR, 2 µg of total RNA were reverse transcribed using random hexamer primers (Thermo Scientific™ SO142) and SuperScript™ III Reverse Transcriptase (InvitrogenTM 18080093) per manufacturer’s instructions. PowerUp™ SYBR™ Green Master Mix (Applied BiosystemsTM A25742) with Cre and GroEL control primers were used to amplify samples on the QuantStudio 3 RT-PCR system. For RNA sequencing, 1 µg of total RNA was rRNA-depleted and prepared for sequencing with the NEBNext rRNA Depletion Kit (Bacteria) (NEB #E7850) and NEBNextUltra II RNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina (NEB #E7770) per manufacturer’s instructions. Samples were multiplexed with NEBNext® Multiplex Oligos for Illumina® (NEB #E7600S). Paired-end sequencing was performed using the NextSeq 500/550 High Output Kit v2.5 75 cycles kit (NextSeq 20024906) on the Illumina NextSeq 550 system. Illumina reads were

Membrane vesicle purification and density gradient ultracentrifugation

Cultures were grown as previously described and donor supernatant was extracted. 4.8 mL of donor supernatant was added to Open-Top Thinwall Ultra-Clear tubes (5 mL, Beckman Coulter 344057). Vesicles were concentrated by pelleting at 300,000g x 5 hrs at 4°C with the SW55 Ti rotor (Beckman Coulter 342196) and the Beckman Coulter Optima L-100K ultracentrifuge. Pelleted vesicles were resuspended in 300 uL of LB. For density gradient ultracentrifugation, concentrated vesicles were combined with OptiPrep™ Density Gradient Medium (Sigma- Aldrich D1556) for a final concentration of 45% OptiPrep, and 800 uL was loaded at the bottom of a 5 mL Ultra-Clear tube. 800 uL each of 40%, 35%, 30%, 25%, and 20% Optiprep diluted in 1x PBS were overlayed sequentially on top of the layer of concentrated vesicles. Ultracentrifugation was performed at 200,000g x 21 hrs using the same rotor and ultracentrifuge as before. 400 uL layers were extracted top to bottom, discarding the first and last layer, for a total of 10 layers. To solubilize membranes, pelleted vesicles were treated at 37°C for 1 hour with 1% SDS prior to SDS precipitation by KCl and density gradient ultracentrifugation. Density gradient layers were co-incubated with recipients or prepared for western blotting as previously described. For nano flow cytometry and structured illumination microscopy of concentrated supernatant, 50 mL of supernatant for each sample was centrifuged at 5000 rpm for 30 min at 4° C. The supernatants were transferred to new microfuge tubes and filtered using 0.22 μm filter units. Vesicles were collected by ultracentrifugation (type 45Ti rotor, Optima L-80 XP Ultracentrifuge Beckman Coulter) at 41000 rpm for 16 h at 4° C. Pellets containing isolated vesicles were resuspended in 500 ml PBS 1X (filtered using 0.02 μm filter units) and stored at 4° C. All fractions of isolated vesicles were verified by fluorescence microscopy (using the FM4-64 membrane dye (Thermofisher scientific # T13320)). All experiments were replicated a minimum of three times in the laboratory.

Cryo-electron tomography

Density gradient samples were mixed with 10 nm diameter colloidal gold beads (used as fiducial markers in image alignment) and deposited onto freshly glow-discharged, lacey carbon film grids for 1 min. The grids were then blotted with filter paper and rapidly frozen in liquid ethane, using a gravity-driven plunger apparatus. Frozen-hydrated specimens were imaged using a 200 keV Thermo Scientific Glacios® Cryo-Transmission Electron Microscope equipped with Falcon 4i Direct Electron Detector. The microscope was operated at 200 kV with a magnification of ×49,000, resulting in an effective pixel size of 2.56 Å at the specimen level. We used software TOMO to collect low-dose, single-axis tilt series with dose fractionation mode at about 6 µm defocus. Tilt series were collected from -51° to 51° with increment of 3° and a cumulative dose of ~80 e− /Å2 distributed over 35 stacks. Each stack contains ~7 images. We used IMOD to facilitate data processing, which includes drift correction of dose-fractionated data and assembly of corrected sums into tilt series, automatic fiducial seed model generation, alignment and

<!-- Page 42 -->


contrast transfer function correction of tilt series, and weighted back projection (WBP) reconstruction of tilt series into tomograms. Each tomographic reconstruction is 1,024 × 1,024 × 300 pixels in pixel size of 10.24 Å. In total, 5 tomographic reconstructions were made from F2 and F3 DG-UC fractions. Imaging was performed on two independent biological replicates simultaneously.

Cryogenic Correlative Light and Electron Microscopy (cryo-CLEM) and Cryogenic Electron Tomography (Cryo-ET) on Cre-mVenus-positive vesicles

F2-F3 (after density gradient ultracentrifugation) and P1 fractions were prepared from CremVenus+ cultures. They were then frozen, shipped overnight on dry ice, and stored at -80 °C in preparation for cryo-CLEM analysis. The sample was subsequently thawed once and vitrified on EM grids as previously described (74) using a Leica EM GP2 plunger freezer. Briefly, 4 μL of suspended vesicles were mixed with 10 nm gold fiducials and loaded onto glow-discharged EM grids (R2/2 Quantifoil Carbon membrane on a Cu 300 mesh). Grids were back blotted and plunged into liquid ethane/propane mixture maintained at -188 °C. Grids were then clipped into the autogrid setup and kept vitreous throughout the various imaging steps and storage. Cryo-LM imaging of mVenus signal was performed as z-stacks using 3.6% of 488 nm laser and a GaAsP- PMT detector on a Zeiss LSM900 confocal microscope (Carl Zeiss Inc., Oberkochen, Germany) equipped with a Linkam CMS196v3 cryostage (Linkam Scientific Instruments Ltd., Redhill, United Kingdom). The lower laser power ensured that the sample remained vitreous during imaging. A 100x air objective with an NA of 0.75 was used for imaging, resulting in a point spread function (PSF) of ~430 nm for mVenus signal (emission wavelength of mVenus is ~527 nm); lateral resolution (XY) by Rayleigh criterion = Nau x 0.61 x l / NA, where Nau is the pin hole size in Airy unit and l is the emission wavelength. Fluorescence targets were evaluated for the presence of mVenus signal by comparing their total intensity to that of the background. The focal plane for each of the targets was chosen out of the z-stack for this calculation. SNR was also calculated for each of the targets; SNR = (Mean target signal - mean background signal) / standard deviation of background signal. Cryo-EM and cryo-ET imaging was performed on a ThermoFisher Krios G3i equipped with a cold stage and a 300 keV field emission gun. Images were acquired using SerialEM software (76) on a K3 direct electron detector (Gatan Inc., Pleasanton, CA, USA) operated in the electron-counted mode. Gatan Imaging Filter (Gatan Inc., Pleasanton, CA, USA) with a range of slit widths (20 – 100 eV) was used to increase contrast at various magnifications. The workflow for cryo-CLEM and cryo-ET is as follows. We first assessed the sample by cryo-EM using magnifications ranging for 82 X, all the way up to 19500 X – we took caution to keep electron radiation damage to negligibly low levels during this initial cryo-EM screening. We then imaged the sample by cryo-LM to assess the distribution of mVenus signal and to identify fluorescent foci that are likely compatible with cryo-EM imaging based on our previous assessments. The sample was re-imaged by cryo-EM to locate the same fluorescent signals. Correlations were performed within SerialEM to sufficient accuracy that ensured capturing the target of interest within the field of view, even at the highest magnification of interest (corresponding to correlation accuracy of 500 nm or better). These targets were then subjected to bi-directional tilt series acquisition with a span of 120° (−60° to +60°) with 2° increments at a magnification of 19500X or 26,000X (corresponding pixel sizes were 4.54 Å and 3.37 Å, respectively) with a defocus of −5 μm and a slit width of 20 eV. The cumulative dose of each tilt-series was less than 100 e−/Å2. Post acquisition, high-precision correlations were performed between cryo-LM and cryo-EM images at progressively higher magnifications using the Zen Connect software (Carl Zeiss Inc., Oberkochen, Germany) – this improved the

6


<!-- Page 43 -->


correlation accuracy to better than a couple of 100 nm. Tilt-series were then aligned using fiducials in etomo within the IMOD package (77) and tomograms were reconstructed using the SIRT-like filter with 10 iterations. In order to illustrate the cryo-CLEM process and cryo-ET analysis, we have presented overlays of cryo-LM and cryo-EM images at an intermediate magnification, along with a slice through the final reconstructed tomogram. Imaging was performed on two independent biological replicates simultaneously.

To threshold vesicles and Cre-mVenus signal, masks were created with Renyi entropy and the watershed function was used for segmentation. Minimum area of signal of both FM4-64 and mVenus to be considered for particle analysis was set at 0.065 µm2. Single-cell transcriptomics

Donors and loxP-mScarlet recipients were co-incubated at a cfu ratio of 1:10 as previously described. After co-incubation, cells were recovered for one hour in MinA media supplemented with 0.2% glucose and 1 mM MgSO4. Bacteria were harvested and scRNA-seq was performed using the smRandom-seq technology (78) without running the Cas9-based step for the depletion of ribosomal RNA (rRNA)-derived amplified and barcoded cDNA. Briefly, DNA primers were conjugated to hydrogel beads and then barcoded using a 3-round, split-pool ligation, allowing a total barcode multiplicity of 96 x 48 x 48, with the UMI and dT tail added on the last round of ligation. Cells were fixed, permeabilized, and quantified, and two technical replicates were pooled. In-situ reverse transcription and dA tailing were performed. Cells, barcoding buffer, barcoded beads, and a continuous oil phase were flowed through the respective channels of a cell and bead encapsulation device (79). Droplets encapsulating cells and beads were collected and thermocycled to barcode cells. Droplet emulsions were broken to harvest barcoded cDNA, the sequencing library was prepared using TruSeq chemistry, and 150 bp paired-end sequencing was performed using Illumina’s NovaSeq X platform. Reads were quality-checked, trimmed, and binned according to unique cell barcodes. Reads were aligned to the Escherichia coli MG1655 genome appended with cre, mScarlet, and msGFP2 sequences.
